title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs
authors: Stanislas Pamela, Nicolas Pailliez, Emmanuel Franck, Victor Michel-Dansac, Laurent Navoret, Vignesh Gopakumar
abstract: Research in the domain of Physics-Informed Neural Networks applied to PDE modelling has advanced significantly in recent years, providing a wide ecosystem of novel methods. However, one frequent limitation is the inability of PINNs to scale out on High-Performance Computing architectures to address more ambitious challenges, particularly non-linear physics models with turbulent dynamics in large spatial domains. Typical studies restrain demonstrations to toy models with simple physics equations, few variables, and rarely any complex non-linear dynamics evolved over long timescales. Part of the AI community has even adopted the idea that "PINNs don't scale". This work proves otherwise. We present a mathematically robust formulation of Finite-Element-Method for Neural Networks (FEM-NN) implemented into a comprehensive, modular framework: Fuse-PINN. This formulation provides the basis for a sclable parallelisation of Physics-Informed Neural Networks on GPU-based HPC systems. Furthermore, an Energy Natural Gradient Descent optimiser is implemented to allow high-precision convergence. Fuse-PINN is demonstrated on physics models relevant to Magnetic Confinement Fusion, including non-linear convective models with fine-scale dynamics. Near-perfect scaling is achieved on multi-GPU runs with increasing problem size.

infographic.key_insight: Fuse-PINN combines finite-element methods and physics-informed neural networks to enable scalable multi-GPU simulation of nonlinear PDEs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a route to GPU-parallel engineering PDE simulation, demonstrated on magnetic-confinement fusion models rather than solid mechanics.
method: Formulate neural-network PDE models within a finite-element framework.
Distribute computation across GPU-based HPC systems.
Use Energy Natural Gradient Descent for high-precision convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports near-perfect multi-GPU scaling as problem size increases, with demonstrations on nonlinear convective models exhibiting fine-scale dynamics.
infographic.watch_item: Increasing-problem-size scaling does not establish fixed-problem speedups or accuracy and cost advantages over conventional FEM solvers.
infographic.paper_title: Fuse-PINN: Combining Finite Element Methods and Physics-Informed Neural Networks to enable massively parallel simulations of non-linear PDEs

title: Thermodynamically consistent neural constitutive models for elastoplasticity via eigen-representations
authors: Harikrishnan Vijayakumaran, Shunyu Yin, Martin Abendroth, Miguel A. Bessa, Karl A. Kalina
abstract: Neural network material models can represent yield surfaces and hardening laws with far more flexibility than classical closed-form plasticity formulations, but training such a model end-to-end through an implicit return map introduces non-trivial challenges. This work presents a thermodynamically consistent neural constitutive model for rate-independent, isotropic elastoplasticity that jointly learns a flexible yield function together with its evolution laws. For non-associative flow, the yield function extends the convex flow potential by a jointly trained additive term, which renders the model thermodynamically consistent by construction. Isotropy and convexity are enforced simultaneously across all learnable components through a permutation-invariant, spectral (eigenvalue-based) representation. Training proceeds through a backward-Euler return map, with gradients propagated by the implicit function theorem together with an eigenvalue-degeneracy-aware scheme for safe differentiation. The robustness and generality of the approach are demonstrated by reproducing known constitutive models, including non-associative flow, learning material behavior from stress--strain data extracted from a full-field finite element simulation, and capturing unknown non-associative behavior from homogenized representative volume elements of a foam. Finally, the proposed neural plasticity model is evaluated within finite element simulations to solve boundary-value-problem under plane stress.

infographic.key_insight: An eigenvalue-based neural constitutive model jointly learns yield behavior and evolution laws for isotropic elastoplasticity while enforcing thermodynamic consistency, including non-associative flow.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables flexible, data-driven plasticity models to be integrated into finite element simulations of boundary-value problems.
method: Use permutation-invariant spectral representations to enforce isotropy and convexity across learnable components.
Construct the non-associative yield function by adding a jointly learned term to a convex flow potential.
Train through a backward-Euler return map using implicit differentiation and eigenvalue-degeneracy-aware gradients.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation includes reproducing known constitutive models, learning from full-field finite element stress–strain data and homogenized foam RVEs, and deployment in plane-stress finite element simulations.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation requires careful handling of implicit return-map differentiation near repeated eigenvalues; the stated scope is rate-independent, isotropic elastoplasticity.
infographic.paper_title: Thermodynamically consistent neural constitutive models for elastoplasticity via eigen-representations

title: Making Plasticity Visible: A Case Study for High-Temperature Exposed Aluminum Alloy
authors: Bakhtiyar Mammadli, Karol Frydrych, Casim Yazici, Azad Mammadli, Kazimierz Skrobas, Siddharth Suman
abstract: Understanding the onset of plastic deformation and the early development of strain localization is essential for characterizing material behavior and identifying failure-prone regions. However, these transitions are not always distinguishable from conventional full-field strain measurements. This study investigates a data- driven framework combining Digital Image Correlation (DIC) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract temporal and spatial deformation signatures during uniaxial tensile loading. The methodology is evaluated using AA6063-T5 aluminum alloy specimens in the as-received condition and following thermal exposure at 100~$^\circ$C, 200~$^\circ$C, and 300~$^\circ$C. PCA applied to sequential strain fields reveals a characteristic peak in the second principal component projection near the yielding transition, showing agreement with the conventional 0.2\% offset criterion across the investigated conditions. Furthermore, principal component maps extracted from high-temporal-resolution strain fields preceding this transition highlight localized deformation features associated with subsequent failure regions. These features are more clearly distinguishable than competing strain concentrations in the corresponding instantaneous strain maps. The results indicate that PCA-derived deformation signatures remain identifiable despite thermally induced variations in mechanical response. This approach demonstrates the potential of unsupervised dimensionality reduction for extracting physically interpretable information on plastic deformation and early strain localization from experimental full-field measurements.

infographic.key_insight: PCA of full-field strain measurements reveals signatures of yielding and early strain localization that are less distinct in instantaneous strain maps.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help identify plasticity onset and failure-prone regions in aluminum components with different thermal exposure histories.
method: Measure sequential strain fields using Digital Image Correlation during uniaxial tensile loading.
Apply unsupervised Principal Component Analysis to extract temporal signatures and spatial deformation maps.
Compare the second-component projection peak with 0.2% offset yielding and inspect pre-transition localization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on AA6063-T5 in as-received and 100°C, 200°C, and 300°C exposed conditions showed agreement between the second-component peak and offset yielding, while pre-transition component maps highlighted subsequent failure regions.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish generalization beyond this alloy and loading mode; early-localization analysis also relies on high-temporal-resolution strain measurements.
infographic.paper_title: Making Plasticity Visible: A Case Study for High-Temperature Exposed Aluminum Alloy

title: Unified constitutive model of body-centered cubic metals informed by discrete dislocation dynamics
authors: Jiarui Zhang, Yin Zhang
abstract: Predicting plastic flow in body-centered cubic metals across temperature and strain-rate regimes requires distinguishing structural resistance from kinetic contributions. Here, we develop a temperature dependent mobility law for screw dislocation, integrating thermal activation theory and relativistic effects. Through discrete dislocation dynamics simulations, uniaxial tension and compression simulations were conducted on configurations with different initial dislocation densities, elucidating the correlation between plastic strain rate and key parameters such as stress, temperature, and dislocation density. Subsequently, a unified constitutive model incorporating temperature and strain rate is derived based on microscopic mechanisms. The model naturally bridges microscopic mechanisms to continuum response, resolving the additivity dilemma by establishing explicit physical criteria for how structural resistances and competing kinetic mechanisms superimpose. Through rigorous bottom-up simulations, we quantitatively capture the crossover point where phonon drag overtakes thermal activation, providing a mechanism-based explanation of anomalous thermal hardening. This work enables physically consistent predictions of strength and creep behavior across broad temperature and strain-rate regimes, advancing beyond phenomenological descriptions toward transparent, mechanism-based alloy design.

infographic.key_insight: A mechanism-based constitutive model links dislocation-scale physics to BCC metal plasticity, distinguishing structural resistance from thermal activation and phonon drag.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model supports strength and creep predictions across temperature and strain-rate regimes, including anomalous thermal hardening.
method: Develop a temperature-dependent screw-dislocation mobility law combining thermal activation and relativistic effects.
Run discrete dislocation dynamics tension and compression simulations at different initial dislocation densities.
Derive a unified constitutive model with physical criteria for combining structural and kinetic resistance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports bottom-up simulations that quantify the crossover from thermal activation to phonon-drag-dominated flow, but provides no numerical accuracy metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental validation and transferability across specific BCC metals are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Unified constitutive model of body-centered cubic metals informed by discrete dislocation dynamics

title: A scaling law for numerical computation of fracture stress intensity factors
authors: Ronghao Cui, Jan Martin Nordbotten, Ivar Stefansson, Inga Berre
abstract: Numerical simulations of fracture propagation require accurate computation of stress intensity factors (SIFs) to determine whether a pre-existing fracture will propagate. Even though displacement solutions from well-established numerical methods generally converge with mesh refinement, the convergence behavior of SIF estimates remains less understood. In this work, we propose a scaling law to improve the performance of SIF extraction using two-point displacement correlation methods. This scaling law relates sampling distance from the fracture tip to mesh resolution. It is developed by balancing the asymptotic truncation error against the numerical discretization error. Three numerical discretization methods--standard quadratic finite elements, quadratic finite elements with quarter-point elements, and a multi-point stress approximation finite volume method--are employed to validate the proposed scaling law on fracture benchmark problems under pure-mode and mixed-mode loading. We find that the conventional nearest-tip sampling strategy fails to compute convergent SIF estimates. In contrast, the proposed scaling-based approach yields decreasing errors in the SIF estimates as the mesh is refined. Across all three discretization methods, the proposed scaling law captures the sampling locations required for convergent SIF extraction, suggesting a general numerical characteristic of near-tip SIF extraction.

infographic.key_insight: Linking fracture-tip sampling distance to mesh resolution enables convergent stress intensity factor estimates where conventional nearest-tip sampling fails.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More reliable stress intensity factors support accurate predictions of whether pre-existing fractures will propagate.
method: Extract stress intensity factors using two-point displacement correlation.
Balance asymptotic truncation error against numerical discretization error to derive a sampling-distance scaling law.
Validate with quadratic finite elements, quarter-point finite elements, and a multi-point stress approximation finite volume method.
infographic.evidence_signal: Pure-mode and mixed-mode fracture benchmarks showed decreasing stress intensity factor errors under mesh refinement with scaling-based sampling across all three discretization methods.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify the scaling formula or implementation constants; these must be checked before applying the method.
infographic.paper_title: A scaling law for numerical computation of fracture stress intensity factors

title: Machine learning of strength surfaces enables high regularization length phase-field fracture
authors: S Chockalingam, Aditya Kumar, Adrian Buganza Tepole
abstract: Classical phase-field models of brittle fracture capture toughness-controlled crack growth but not the material's strength surface, which governs crack nucleation. The theory of Kumar et al. (2020) incorporates the strength surface through a nucleation driving force, and Chockalingam (2025) derived this driving force for arbitrary strength surfaces described by $n$ material parameters, with which the phase-field strength surface (PFSS) converges to the material strength surface as the regularization length $\varepsilon \to 0$ and matches it exactly at $n$ chosen states for any $\varepsilon$. In practice, however, the strength surface must be supplied as an analytic form chosen and calibrated case by case, and for the widely used analytic surfaces ($n=2$) accurate strength reproduction requires $\varepsilon$ commensurate with the Irwin characteristic length $l_{ch}$, imposing prohibitive mesh requirements for large structures. We introduce a neural-network (NN) strength function that is learned directly from strength data, is physics-constrained by construction, and provides far more calibration parameters than analytic surfaces; the calibration is generalized to any number of strength states and to enforce openness in chosen directions. A single architecture captures synthetic data from the Mohr-Coulomb, Drucker-Prager, Mogi-Coulomb and 3D Hoek-Brown surfaces and experimental data for graphite, natural rubber and styrene-butadiene rubber. The resulting PFSS is accurate up to $\varepsilon = 10\,l_{ch}$, whereas that of the exact analytic surfaces performs comparatively poorly even at $\varepsilon = 0.5\,l_{ch}$. Finite-element simulations validate the theory across fracture regimes. By decoupling strength fidelity from the regularization length, the approach substantially reduces the mesh resolution required for phase-field fracture simulations of large structures.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-constrained neural-network strength function preserves accurate phase-field strength surfaces at regularization lengths up to 10 times the Irwin characteristic length.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Decoupling strength accuracy from regularization length reduces mesh-resolution demands for phase-field fracture simulations of large structures.
method: Learn the material strength function directly from data using a physics-constrained neural network.
Calibrate the nucleation driving force against multiple strength states and enforce openness in selected directions.
Embed the learned strength function in phase-field fracture simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests cover four synthetic strength surfaces, experimental data for graphite and two rubbers, and finite-element fracture simulations; learned surfaces remain accurate up to ε = 10 l_ch, while analytic counterparts perform comparatively poorly even at ε = 0.5 l_ch.
infographic.watch_item: Reliability beyond the sampled strength states and loading regimes requires validation, particularly when selecting directions in which the strength surface remains open.
infographic.paper_title: Machine learning of strength surfaces enables high regularization length phase-field fracture

title: A mesh-free deep energy method for phase-field modeling of thermally driven brittle fracture
authors: Han Zhang, Mehrisadat Makki Alamdari, Babak Shahbodagh, Mohammad Vahab, Cosmin Anitescu, Timon Rabczuk
abstract: Phase-field simulation of thermally driven fracture requires resolving localized crack bands whose paths are unknown in advance and thermal boundary layers whose thickness evolves during the transient. Neural energy-based computations of thermal fracture have so far started from defects placed in advance. This paper proposes a mesh-free deep energy method based on multiresolution neural representations that predicts spontaneous crack nucleation, crack spacing, and selective crack propagation and arrest under transient thermal loading. Two networks, each with its own multiresolution encoding, represent the displacement and phase fields and the transient temperature, and the mechanical energy and the incremental functional of the backward Euler heat equation are estimated on integration points redrawn at every iteration. Restricting irreversibility to the crack set, carrying the optimizer state across load steps and decaying the learning rates within each step help prevent spurious damage accumulation. On two notched plates the initiation peak loads agree closely with an independent finite element reference. On a quenched glass strip under an analytical temperature field the crack path changes from straight to oscillatory and then to branched, with an oscillation threshold close to the linear stability prediction. Under a prescribed boundary temperature a quenched ceramic slab forms a crack array of the type observed in experiment, with a spacing close to that of a published benchmark. On the slab and a quenched annulus the arrays are denser than those of a finite element computation on the same material field. No crack paths, nucleation sites or crack-adapted meshes are prescribed.

infographic.key_insight: A mesh-free deep energy method predicts thermally driven crack nucleation, spacing, propagation and arrest without prescribing crack paths or nucleation sites.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support thermal-shock assessment of brittle components with evolving temperature gradients and initially unknown fracture patterns.
method: Use separate multiresolution neural networks for displacement–phase fields and transient temperature.
Minimize mechanical energy and a backward Euler thermal functional using integration points resampled each iteration.
Restrict irreversibility to the crack set, retain optimizer state across load steps and decay learning rates within each step.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests show close agreement with finite element initiation peak loads on two notched plates, an oscillation threshold near linear stability predictions in quenched glass, and ceramic-slab crack spacing near a published benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: Slab and annulus crack arrays are denser than finite element predictions on the same material field, leaving crack-density agreement unresolved.
infographic.paper_title: A mesh-free deep energy method for phase-field modeling of thermally driven brittle fracture

title: Dynamic Prandtl-Reuss Thermoplasticity with Degenerating Yield Constraints
authors: Sebastian Owczarek
abstract: We study a three-dimensional dynamic thermoplastic system with a temperature-dependent convex yield set whose deviatoric section may collapse completely at a finite temperature. The underlying constitutive model is rate-independent Prandtl-Reuss perfect plasticity, without Kelvin-Voigt viscosity, hardening, or a safe-load condition. We construct global approximation-generated relaxed entropy-energy states by a one-parameter Temam-Norton-Hoff-Galerkin scheme with an undiscretized heat equation and untruncated plastic heat production. The logarithmic temperature is strongly compact in $L^2(0,T;L^q(Ω))$ for every $q<6$ and in $L^p((0,T)\timesΩ)$ for every $p<8/3$. An entropy-weighted work estimate yields convergence of the overstress at rate $O(\sqrt{\log n/n})$ in every fixed finite Lebesgue space and identifies stress admissibility. The constitutive limit comprises a distributional plastic balance, finite support-weighted measures, and compact-fibre lifts carrying exact normality and maximum plastic work. A locally finite lift on the positive-radius fibres unifies the level-restricted limits at every continuity level. At the macroscopic level, however, the available compactness does not identify a canonical stress-plastic-flow pairing. Moreover, an explicit smooth state satisfying the intrinsic relaxed balance conditions shows that these conditions do not imply macroscopic Prandtl-Reuss normality. In the fully collapsed regime, an energy-entropy rigidity argument determines the evolution and yields approximation-generated examples in which the plastic flow need not be a finite measure or the displacement need not retain its full boundary trace. Thermal concentration and plastic entropy production remain explicit throughout.

infographic.key_insight: Global relaxed entropy-energy states can be constructed for dynamic thermoplasticity even when the temperature-dependent yield set collapses, but macroscopic Prandtl–Reuss normality is not guaranteed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The analysis clarifies what thermoplastic models can predict when heating eliminates shear resistance, without viscosity, hardening, or a safe-load assumption.
method: Use a one-parameter Temam–Norton–Hoff–Galerkin approximation with an undiscretized heat equation and untruncated plastic heating.
Establish logarithmic-temperature compactness and stress admissibility through entropy-weighted estimates.
Represent limiting plastic behavior with support-weighted measures and fibre lifts preserving exact normality.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical results include an overstress convergence rate of O(√(log n/n)) in every fixed finite Lebesgue space and an explicit smooth counterexample to macroscopic normality; the abstract reports no numerical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Available compactness does not identify a canonical macroscopic stress–plastic-flow pairing; complete yield collapse can also permit non-measure plastic flow or loss of the full displacement boundary trace.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamic Prandtl-Reuss Thermoplasticity with Degenerating Yield Constraints

title: A Unified Framework for First- and Second-Order Energy-Stable Parametric Finite Element Methods for Planar Willmore Flow
authors: Xiaoli Li, Yujing Yan
abstract: The construction of structure-preserving schemes for planar Willmore flow that are second-order accurate in time and avoid large coupled nonlinear solves remains challenging. In this work, we develop a unified framework for first- and second-order fully discrete energy-stable parametric finite element schemes for planar Willmore flow with a length-penalization term. The framework is based on a new equivalent reformulation involving a global auxiliary variable. The main novelty lies in the second-order construction, which combines midpoint curvature quantities weighted by elementwise arc-length Jacobian ratios with a compatible discrete tangent to obtain exact discrete chain rules for the bending energy and curve length. A further contribution is to show that both schemes satisfy discrete modified energy dissipation laws that yield the same type of a priori bounds on the discrete solution as the original energy law. They also retain Barrett--Garcke--N{ü}rnberg tangential motion to promote favorable mesh distribution. Each stage reduces to two linear solves with exactly the same coefficient matrix and one scalar nonlinear solve. We rigorously prove unique solvability of the linear subproblems under suitable assumptions and derive computable sufficient conditions for local existence and uniqueness of the scalar solution near unity. Numerical experiments demonstrate the expected temporal accuracy, energy dissipation, good mesh quality and computational efficiency.

infographic.key_insight: A unified parametric finite element framework delivers first- and second-order time integration for planar Willmore flow with provable modified energy dissipation while avoiding large coupled nonlinear solves.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports efficient simulation of planar curve relaxation governed by bending energy and length penalization while promoting good mesh distribution.
method: Reformulate the flow using a global auxiliary variable.
Combine Jacobian-weighted midpoint curvature and a compatible discrete tangent to obtain exact discrete chain rules.
Reduce each stage to two linear solves sharing one coefficient matrix and one scalar nonlinear solve.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments demonstrate the expected temporal accuracy, energy dissipation, good mesh quality and computational efficiency.
infographic.watch_item: Solvability guarantees require suitable assumptions, and scalar-solve existence and uniqueness are local near unity under computable sufficient conditions.
infographic.paper_title: A Unified Framework for First- and Second-Order Energy-Stable Parametric Finite Element Methods for Planar Willmore Flow

title: Ultrasound Elastography: Excitation Methods and Low-Cost Alternative
authors: Corin F. Otesteanu
abstract: Ultrasound elastography (or elasticity imaging) is a method that characterizes the tissue mechanical properties with the purpose of aiding the diagnosis of certain pathologies. Many novel clinical applications use the assumption that these tissue properties are changed in the presence of pathological processes. Characterization of tissue mechanical properties is achieved by imaging the response of the tissue to an induced stress or excitation. A plethora of approaches have been used in the scientific community to induce excitation in tissue, which usually require additional tools or devices than are costly. Furthermore these are usually integrated in the imaging pipeline using additional software or hardware for control. An alternative that is simpler, faster to integrate (and low-cost) is proposed in this work, by using readily available smartphones as a source of mechanical excitation. The induced displacements are used to solve the elasticity inverse problem (IP) using a finite element method (FEM) approach. Preliminary elasticity reconstructions of a phantom that mimics tissue are similar to when using a dedicated actuator as means of inducing harmonic displacements, illustrating the feasibility of our low-cost ultrasound elasography approach.

infographic.key_insight: Readily available smartphones can provide low-cost mechanical excitation for ultrasound elastography, with preliminary phantom reconstructions similar to those obtained using a dedicated actuator.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Smartphone excitation could reduce hardware costs and simplify integration of tissue-stiffness imaging systems.
method: Use a smartphone to induce mechanical excitation in a tissue-mimicking phantom.
Image the induced tissue displacements with ultrasound.
Solve the elasticity inverse problem using a finite element method.
infographic.evidence_signal: Preliminary tissue-mimicking phantom tests produced elasticity reconstructions described as similar to those obtained with a dedicated harmonic actuator, without quantitative metrics in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: Feasibility is demonstrated only in preliminary phantom tests; clinical accuracy and excitation reproducibility remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Ultrasound Elastography: Excitation Methods and Low-Cost Alternative

title: Physics-constrained differentiable causal discovery of constitutive mechanisms through boundary value problems
authors: Michael A. Kraus
abstract: Data-driven constitutive model discovery is recast as causal discovery of mechanism parent sets using time-unrolled structural causal models. Hard-coding balance laws and constitutive skeletons, candidate graphs score environment--mechanism and state--state edges via weak-form equilibrium gaps evaluated from full-field displacements, avoiding the need to measure stresses or internal variables. An adaptive lasso and a NOTEARS-type constraint ensure graph acyclicity and an explicit evaluation order, treating climate-chamber protocols as interventions. Automatic differentiation yields the score's Gauss--Newton matrix as a local identifiability certificate, driving greedy D-optimal test design. In a synthetic study on a hygro-thermo-viscoelastic damaging plate (8 true edges among 13 candidates), interventional data recover the exact true graph in 7 of 10 runs (0.01px displacement noise) with zero attribution error. Conversely, observational data with a temperature--moisture correlation of $-0.998$ fail entirely because confounded scores are 250--380 times flatter. Observationally discovered models reproduce training climates (3.6% error) but mispredict hot and humid climates by up to 41.5% (16.9% average), whereas interventionally discovered models stay within 3.2%. A correlation sweep shows the certificate successfully predicts attribution errors, though weak-form score noise bias remains a primary limitation. Computed without knowledge of the truth, the D-optimal design selects test sets ranked second or third out of 126 candidates.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-constrained causal discovery can identify constitutive mechanism dependencies from displacement fields, while correlated observational data can hide the correct attribution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Climate-chamber interventions can help build constitutive models that generalize to unseen environments without measuring stresses or internal variables.
method: Embed balance laws and constitutive skeletons in time-unrolled causal models scored by weak-form equilibrium gaps.
Use adaptive lasso and a NOTEARS-type acyclicity constraint to select mechanism dependencies.
Compute a Gauss–Newton identifiability certificate via automatic differentiation to guide greedy D-optimal test design.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a synthetic plate with 8 true edges among 13 candidates, interventional data recovered the exact graph in 7/10 runs at 0.01-pixel displacement noise; prediction errors stayed within 3.2%, versus up to 41.5% for observationally discovered models in hot, humid climates.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is synthetic, and noise bias in the weak-form score remains a primary limitation.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-constrained differentiable causal discovery of constitutive mechanisms through boundary value problems

title: Mechanical behaviour of the intact brain-skull interface under tension, compression and shear
authors: Sajjad Arzemanzadeh, Karol Miller, Ron Kikinis, Adam Wittek
abstract: The brain-skull interface governs the boundary/contact conditions of the brain in computational head models, yet its mechanical behaviour remains poorly characterised experimentally. We characterised the brain-skull interface by testing brain-skull complex samples (skull bone, meninges and brain tissue in their native arrangement) excised from 19 sheep cadaver heads under uniaxial tension and compression at strain rates of 0.002, 0.02 and 0.2 s$^{-1}$ and simple shear at 0.02 s$^{-1}$. Histology confirmed that the meningeal layers remained intact and attached to the brain and skull after excision. We acquired magnetic resonance images of every sample, reconstructed their geometry and developed a sample-specific finite element model of each experiment. We represented the brain tissue using a second-order Ogden hyperelastic model and the brain-skull interface using a cohesive zone model. Using inverse finite element analysis, we first calibrated the brain tissue parameters for each subject. Keeping these parameters fixed, we then identified the interface parameters from the corresponding brain-skull complex specimen. The brain tissue shear modulus increased with strain rate from 0.94 $\pm$ 0.16 kPa at 0.002 s$^{-1}$ to 1.60 $\pm$ 0.30 kPa at 0.2 s$^{-1}$. In contrast, the interface properties (maximum normal traction 2.35 $\pm$ 0.81 kPa, maximum tangential traction 4.14 $\pm$ 0.97 kPa, and fracture energy 0.35 $\pm$ 0.14 N m$^{-1}$) showed no significant dependence on strain rate or loading mode. In all samples, failure occurred within the subarachnoid space. Neither a rigid brain-skull connection nor frictionless sliding contact with separation reproduced the measured mechanical response or failure mode of the brain-skull interface. Our experimentally derived cohesive zone model provides a realistic representation of the brain-skull interface for computational head models.

infographic.key_insight: The intact brain–skull interface is better represented by a cohesive zone model than by rigid attachment or frictionless sliding, with failure occurring within the subarachnoid space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Experimentally calibrated interface properties can improve boundary and contact conditions in computational head models.
method: Test native brain–skull specimens from 19 sheep cadaver heads under tension, compression and shear.
Use MRI-derived geometry to build specimen-specific finite element models.
Apply inverse finite element analysis to calibrate Ogden brain tissue parameters, then cohesive interface parameters.
infographic.evidence_signal: Brain shear modulus increased from 0.94 to 1.60 kPa across tested strain rates, while interface properties showed no significant rate or loading-mode dependence: peak normal traction 2.35 ± 0.81 kPa, peak tangential traction 4.14 ± 0.97 kPa and fracture energy 0.35 ± 0.14 N/m.
infographic.watch_item: Parameters derived from sheep cadaver specimens require validation before use in human head models or extrapolation beyond the tested loading rates.
infographic.paper_title: Mechanical behaviour of the intact brain-skull interface under tension, compression and shear

title: Adapting a Vision Foundation Model for Fracture Characterization in Acoustic Image Logs
authors: Guangyu Wang, Xiaodong Ma, Xinming Wu
abstract: Natural fractures (NFs) and drilling-induced tensile fractures (DITFs) in acoustic image logs provide insights into rock mass structure and in situ stress, but manual characterization is time-consuming. Deep learning can automate this task, although expert-labeled data are scarce. We investigate whether adapting a pretrained vision foundation model (VFM) outperforms task-specific models trained from scratch with limited annotations. Using 80 annotated acoustic image samples, we fine-tuned DINOv3, pretrained on satellite imagery, and evaluated it on four boreholes excluded from fine-tuning. The adapted model estimated NF and DITF parameters comparably to human interpretation. Relative to U-Net, YOLOv8, and Swin Transformer models trained from scratch, it yielded fewer false positives and negatives and more accurate fracture counts and orientations. However, its performance advantage generally narrowed as training sample size decreased. We also assessed decoder architecture, fine-tuning strategy, and image enhancement. A progressive upsampling decoder with full fine-tuning performed best among the DINOv3 configurations tested, while fracture-focused image enhancement did not consistently improve accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of VFM adaptation for fracture characterization in acoustic image logs with limited labeled data and suggest a transferable workflow for other annotation-scarce geoscientific imaging tasks.

infographic.key_insight: Adapting pretrained DINOv3 improved fracture characterization in acoustic image logs over task-specific models trained from scratch with limited annotations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated characterization of natural and drilling-induced tensile fractures can support rock mass assessment and in situ stress interpretation while reducing manual analysis.
method: Fine-tune satellite-imagery-pretrained DINOv3 on annotated acoustic image logs.
Compare against U-Net, YOLOv8, and Swin Transformer models trained from scratch.
Test decoder designs, fine-tuning strategies, and fracture-focused image enhancement.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 80 annotated samples and four boreholes excluded from fine-tuning, adapted DINOv3 estimated fracture parameters comparably to human interpretation and produced fewer detection errors than the scratch-trained baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The performance advantage generally narrowed as training sample size decreased, and fracture-focused image enhancement did not consistently improve accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Adapting a Vision Foundation Model for Fracture Characterization in Acoustic Image Logs

title: Numerical analysis of coupled flow, deformation and frictional contact mechanics in a fractured porous medium
authors: Marius Nevland, Kundan Kumar, Inga Berre, Jakub Wiktor Both, Eirik Keilegavlen
abstract: This paper studies the numerical approximation of a mathematical model of coupled flow and viscoelastic deformation in a fractured porous medium including fracture contact mechanics. We consider a mixed-dimensional model, where the fracture is modeled as a co-dimension one object within the porous medium. This model couples Darcy flow in the matrix and fracture, linear viscoelasticity of the matrix and frictional contact mechanics of the fracture surfaces; the contact conditions include normal compliance and a Coulomb friction law. We propose and analyze a fully discrete numerical scheme for this problem, using conformal finite elements in space and the implicit Euler method in time. Existence and uniqueness of the discrete solution is established, and stability and a priori error estimates are derived. A numerical experiment is performed in which numerical error estimates are computed and compared to the theoretical results.

infographic.key_insight: A fully discrete mixed-dimensional scheme couples porous flow, viscoelastic deformation and frictional fracture contact, with proven discrete existence, uniqueness, stability and a priori error estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports simulation of fractured porous materials where fluid flow, deformation and fracture sliding interact.
method: Couple matrix and fracture Darcy flow with linear viscoelastic matrix deformation.
Represent fractures as co-dimension-one interfaces with normal compliance and Coulomb friction.
Discretize using conforming finite elements in space and implicit Euler time stepping.
infographic.evidence_signal: A numerical experiment computes discretization errors and compares them with the theoretical estimates.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports one numerical experiment, leaving broad practical validation of the model unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical analysis of coupled flow, deformation and frictional contact mechanics in a fractured porous medium

title: A pseudostress-based fully mixed finite element method for the stationary Biot--Poisson--Nernst--Planck system
authors: Cristian Inzunza
abstract: We develop a pseudostress-based fully mixed finite element method for the stationary Biot-Poisson-Nernst-Planck system describing ionic transport in a charged, saturated, and deformable porous medium. The mechanical equations are reformulated in terms of a non-symmetric pseudostress and the solid displacement, while mixed formulations are retained for the Darcy, electrostatic, and ionic equations. The nonlinear electrostatic and advective couplings are treated in a Banach space setting. The formulation provides direct approximations of the pseudostress, fluxes, and concentration gradients, and permits algebraic reconstruction of the displacement gradient and Cauchy stress. Under block-stability and small-data assumptions, we establish continuous and discrete well-posedness, with poroelastic stability bounds uniform with respect to the first Lame parameter. A conforming Raviart-Thomas discretization, completed by discontinuous polynomials, yields a priori error estimates and convergence rates. For the coupled scheme in two dimensions, we construct a residual-based a posteriori error estimator and establish its reliability under an additional smallness condition on the prescribed data. Local efficiency is proved for polynomial boundary data, with boundary-data oscillation included for general traces. We also describe the estimator modifications for nonhomogeneous displacement and normal-flux data under corresponding stability and solvability hypotheses. Numerical experiments examine convergence of the mixed and reconstructed fields, robustness in the nearly incompressible regime, adaptive refinement, and ionic polarization in a charged porous medium.

infographic.key_insight: A pseudostress-based fully mixed finite element method couples porous-solid deformation, fluid flow, electrostatics, and ionic transport while retaining stability near incompressibility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation supports simulation of charged, deformable porous media with direct flux approximations and algebraically reconstructed Cauchy stress.
method: Reformulate mechanics using non-symmetric pseudostress and displacement, with mixed Darcy, electrostatic, and ionic equations.
Discretize using conforming Raviart–Thomas elements and discontinuous polynomials.
Use a residual-based error estimator to guide adaptive refinement in two dimensions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports well-posedness and error estimates under stated assumptions, plus numerical tests of convergence, near-incompressibility robustness, adaptivity, and ionic polarization.
infographic.watch_item: Well-posedness requires block-stability and small-data assumptions; estimator reliability requires an additional smallness condition, and general boundary traces introduce oscillation terms.
infographic.paper_title: A pseudostress-based fully mixed finite element method for the stationary Biot--Poisson--Nernst--Planck system

title: Patient-specific Modeling of the Tricuspid Valve from 3D Transesophageal Echocardiography
authors: Davide Tondi, Vijay K. Dubey, Collin E. Haese, Colton J. Kostelnik, Mrudang Mathur, Sumedh Seetharam
abstract: Purpose: Image-based patient-specific simulations of the tricuspid valve (TV) could support repair planning. However, clinical images incompletely resolve the chordal anatomy and cannot directly determine tissue properties, which hinders the development of such models. We developed and evaluated a framework that simulates the TV from clinical images and addresses these limitations using measurements on explanted human valves. Methods: We reconstructed ten functionally competent human TVs from 3D transesophageal echocardiography. Following manual segmentation, we automatically built finite element models with synthetic chordae and with leaflet thickness, chordal insertion density, and tissue properties informed by ex vivo human measurements. Next, we used shape matching and force-based chordal-length adjustment to simulate valve closure. We also assessed inter-observer segmentation variability and sensitivity to chordal insertion density, leaflet stiffness, leaflet thickness, and chordal size and material properties. Results: Per-valve median geometric errors were 0.61-1.13 mm relative to the morphed references and 0.55-0.95 mm relative to the image-derived surfaces. Coaptation covered 20-42% of the leaflet area, and median leaflet stresses ranged from 7.6 to 16.9 kPa. Inter-observer variability in segmentation most strongly affected coaptation area. Of the population-based inputs, insertion density and leaflet stiffness most affected geometric error. Thickness primarily affected stress, whereas chordal size and material properties had limited effects. Conclusion: Clinical echocardiography, supplemented with ex vivo human tissue data, enabled patient-specific simulation of ten human TVs. This framework provides a foundation for investigating valve mechanics and developing repair-planning tools, while sensitivity analyses identify priorities for model refinement and uncertainty assessment.

infographic.key_insight: Patient-specific tricuspid valve finite element models can reproduce valve closure using clinical 3D echocardiography supplemented with ex vivo human tissue measurements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports valve mechanics analysis and future repair-planning tools while identifying modeling inputs that require careful uncertainty assessment.
method: Manually segment 3D transesophageal echocardiography and automatically construct finite element models with synthetic chordae.
Assign leaflet thickness, chordal insertion density, and tissue properties using ex vivo human measurements.
Simulate closure through shape matching and force-based chordal-length adjustment; assess segmentation and parameter sensitivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across ten functionally competent human valves, per-valve median geometric errors were 0.55–0.95 mm against image-derived surfaces, with coaptation covering 20–42% of leaflet area.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation was limited to functionally competent valves; segmentation variability strongly affected coaptation, and pathological-valve repair planning remains unvalidated.
infographic.paper_title: Patient-specific Modeling of the Tricuspid Valve from 3D Transesophageal Echocardiography

title: Quantum algorithmic framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials via efficient block-encoding
authors: Yuki Sato, Ruho Kondo
abstract: Quantum computing offers a promising approach to accelerating large-scale numerical analysis, including the finite element method. However, its practical application requires efficient quantum circuit implementations of discretized linear systems. In this study, we develop a quantum algorithmic framework for two-dimensional isotropic linear elastic materials discretized using the finite element method. The key contribution is an explicit construction of a normalized block-encoding of the shifted global stiffness matrix, which is essential for applying a quantum linear system solver based on the quantum singular value transformation with improved dependence on the condition number. By analytically diagonalizing the element stiffness matrix and expressing the global stiffness matrix through a factorized finite element assembly, we construct the required block-encoding using a constant number of ancilla qubits and a gate complexity logarithmic in the number of degrees of freedom. We further analyze the computational complexity of displacement state preparation, strain energy estimation, and low-resolution displacement reconstruction, identifying conditions under which polynomial quantum speedups may be achieved. Numerical experiments on cantilever beam problems verify the accuracy of the proposed quantum circuits and demonstrate agreement with conventional finite element solutions. These results establish an explicit and resource-efficient quantum framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials.

infographic.key_insight: An explicit, resource-efficient block-encoding enables quantum linear-system solvers for finite element analysis of 2D isotropic linear elastic materials.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could accelerate displacement and strain-energy calculations under suitable conditions for polynomial quantum speedups.
method: Analytically diagonalize the element stiffness matrix and factorize global finite element assembly.
Block-encode the normalized, shifted global stiffness matrix using constant ancilla qubits and gate complexity logarithmic in the degrees of freedom.
Apply a quantum singular value transformation–based linear-system solver and analyze selected output costs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical cantilever-beam experiments verify the proposed quantum circuits and show agreement with conventional finite element solutions.
infographic.watch_item: Efficient block-encoding alone does not guarantee end-to-end speedup; displacement-state preparation and output reconstruction costs must also be considered.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum algorithmic framework for finite element analysis of isotropic linear elastic materials via efficient block-encoding

title: Improved Closed-Form Identification of the Air-Gap Permeance in Magnetic Equivalent Circuits of Rotor-Eccentric Electric Motors
authors: Philip Desenfans
abstract: Fast and accurate simulation of electric motors is essential for their design, fault diagnosis and control. Magnetic equivalent circuits (MECs) offer a computationally efficient alternative to the finite element method (FEM), yet their flux tube representation poorly captures the air-gap field. This creates a challenge, as the air gap stores most of the magnetic energy and governs the electromagnetic torque and, in rotor-eccentric motors, the unbalanced magnetic pull (UMP). Existing air-gap permeance expressions vary widely in their results for torque ripple and UMP and account for tooth-normal eccentricity only. This paper proposes the dual-term air-gap permeance (DTAP) model, a closed-form expression for the air-gap permeance between a stator and a rotor tooth that accounts for tooth-normal and tooth-tangential eccentricity, with and without rotor skew. Its parameters are identified from a FEM model of the air gap and the complete set of tooth heads, which includes the shielding by the neighbouring teeth. For three motors, DTAP reproduces the FEM air-gap permeance with a 2.8-4.8 times smaller error than the state of the art, at a comparable computational cost. Implemented in the MEC of an eccentric induction motor, it reproduces the torque ripple within 1.6% and the peak UMP within 1.3% of the reference, i.e., with 2.8 and 27 times smaller deviations than the state of the art. DTAP thereby enables MEC to predict the torque pulsations and bearing loads of eccentric motors more accurately without sacrificing computational speed.

infographic.key_insight: The dual-term air-gap permeance (DTAP) model improves magnetic equivalent circuit accuracy by capturing both tooth-normal and tooth-tangential rotor eccentricity at comparable computational cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More accurate torque ripple and unbalanced magnetic pull predictions support motor fault diagnosis, control, and bearing-load assessment.
method: Use a closed-form permeance expression between stator and rotor teeth, with or without rotor skew.
Identify parameters using an air-gap FEM model containing all tooth heads to capture neighboring-tooth shielding.
Integrate DTAP into a magnetic equivalent circuit for eccentric-motor simulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three motors, DTAP reduced air-gap permeance error by factors of 2.8–4.8; in an eccentric induction motor, torque ripple and peak unbalanced magnetic pull were within 1.6% and 1.3% of the reference, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Parameter identification requires FEM, and validation across three motors does not establish accuracy for all motor geometries or eccentricity conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Improved Closed-Form Identification of the Air-Gap Permeance in Magnetic Equivalent Circuits of Rotor-Eccentric Electric Motors

title: SiC-BN composites with extreme thermal and environmental stability
authors: Abhijit Biswas, Eugenio Garcia-Granados, Saman Zare, Mozhdeh Mirakhory, JungHun Park, Shuvodeep De
abstract: Ceramic materials that maintain structural integrity and resist thermal-shock under extreme conditions are critical for many applications. Here we show that spark plasma sintered composites containing equal weight fractions of hexagonal silicon carbide (6H-SiC) and boron nitride (h-BN) exhibit exceptional stability under extreme high-temperature oxidizing conditions and unusually stable temperature-independent thermal conductivity across a broad temperature range. Under high-velocity oxygen-fuel torch exposure in air, it withstands prolonged heating and thermal-cycling at surface temperatures reaching >1500 °C, whereas pure 6H-SiC and h-BN rapidly fractures or erodes. Microstructural evaluation shows the formation of a multi-phase surface silica layer that further protects the material from oxidation. Finite-element analysis heat-flux map shows that intrinsic porosity mitigates thermal stress, while ReaxFF molecular dynamics simulations reveal thermally driven interfacial reconstruction and the formation of a Si-N/C-B-rich bonding network, enhancing the interfacial cohesion at elevated temperatures. This lightweight, easily machinable ceramic composite will be a promising structural material in extreme environment applications.

infographic.key_insight: A spark plasma sintered composite with equal weight fractions of 6H-SiC and h-BN withstands extreme oxidizing heat while maintaining unusually temperature-independent thermal conductivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This lightweight, machinable ceramic is a promising candidate for structural components exposed to severe heating and thermal cycling.
method: Spark plasma sintering of equal-weight 6H-SiC and h-BN.
High-velocity oxygen-fuel torch testing and surface microstructural evaluation.
Finite-element heat-flux analysis and ReaxFF molecular dynamics simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The composite survived prolonged torch heating and thermal cycling at surface temperatures above 1500 °C, while pure 6H-SiC and h-BN rapidly fractured or eroded.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify retained mechanical strength or service lifetime, leaving long-term structural durability to be established.
infographic.paper_title: SiC-BN composites with extreme thermal and environmental stability

title: Partition of Unity Data-driven Finite Element Method for Anisotropic Diffusion in Magnetized Plasmas
authors: Siu Wun Cheung, Youngsoo Choi
abstract: Numerical simulation of transport processes in magnetized plasmas is characterized by extreme anisotropy, where diffusion along magnetic field lines can be many orders of magnitude larger than in the perpendicular direction. This anisotropy leads to thin, steep boundary layers and numerical pollution that standard finite element methods struggle to resolve without prohibitive mesh refinement. In this paper, we introduce the Partition of Unity Data-Driven Finite Element Method (PU-DDFEM), a data-driven local model reduction approach, for anisotropic diffusion. The method utilizes a bottom-up construction to enable a complete offline-online splitting. We parametrize the local magnetic field and boundary conditions to generate a snapshot space that captures the essential physics of plasma confinement. Dominant modes are extracted via a local spectral problem to identify representative features. These modes are then mapped to the global domain using a partition of unity to form a conforming approximation space. This ensures that the basis functions are fully reusable across different global magnetic configurations, significantly reducing the online computational overhead for large-scale plasma simulations.

infographic.key_insight: PU-DDFEM builds reusable local reduced bases and combines them through a partition of unity to approximate strongly anisotropic diffusion in magnetized plasmas.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets lower online simulation costs for plasma transport, where extreme anisotropy can make standard finite element mesh refinement prohibitively expensive.
method: Generate local snapshots by parametrizing magnetic fields and boundary conditions.
Extract dominant local modes through a spectral problem.
Assemble a conforming global approximation using partition-of-unity functions with complete offline–online splitting.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes the construction and intended computational benefits but reports no quantitative accuracy results, speedups, or benchmark details.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy for new global magnetic configurations may depend on how well the offline snapshots cover relevant local fields and boundary conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Partition of Unity Data-driven Finite Element Method for Anisotropic Diffusion in Magnetized Plasmas
